Section 1: Week 48 Listening: A Community Garden Meeting

Mia: Hi, Daniel. I'm Mia, the volunteer coordinator. This meeting is to introduce new volunteers to our community garden. We can discuss the timetable, equipment and rules before you decide which team to join.
Daniel: Thanks. Sorry I'm late. The bus was delayed by traffic, so I couldn't get here on time.
Mia: Don't worry. We haven't started the practical work yet. How long have you lived locally?
Daniel: I've been living in the area for about two years, but I only heard about the garden last month. A neighbour suggested it as a way to meet people and spend time outdoors.
Mia: That sounds good. What kind of work would you enjoy?
Daniel: I'm quite good at building things, but I've never grown vegetables before. I've repaired shelves at home and I'm comfortable using tools. I'm happy to learn from someone with more experience.
Mia: Our gardeners can teach you. The main thing is to be reliable. We meet every Saturday morning from nine to eleven. But if it rains, we cancel. There's no covered work area, and the ground becomes slippery.
Daniel: I sometimes have to work on Saturdays. Would that stop me joining?
Mia: No. Even once a month helps. We ask people to tell us when they cannot come, so the team leader can plan the jobs.
Daniel: Do I need my own tools?
Mia: We provide most tools, but you should bring your own gloves. Wear strong shoes too, as the paths can be muddy and uneven. There's a sink by the gate where you can wash afterwards.
Daniel: Is there a membership fee?
Mia: Yes, it's twenty pounds a year. If you can't afford it, we can waive the fee. Money shouldn't prevent anyone from joining. The fee helps us maintain tools and buy seeds.
Daniel: That's reasonable. Which part of the garden needs help?
Mia: There are three teams: vegetables, flowers and compost. The compost area needs the most help. Fewer people want to work there because it's smelly, but good compost keeps the soil healthy.
Daniel: I don't mind that. I could help turn the compost and repair any wooden boxes.
Mia: Excellent. One important rule is that no artificial pesticides or fertilisers are allowed. We only use organic methods. Please ask the team leader before adding anything to the soil.
Daniel: What should I do if the weather is bad next Saturday?
Mia: Check our website. We'll post a message by eight, before people leave home.
Daniel: And what time does the next meeting start?
Mia: Next Saturday at nine, as usual. Come to the gate and I'll introduce you to the team.
Daniel: Thank you. I'm looking forward to starting.

Section 2: Community Garden Workshop: Planning and Problem-Solving

Hello everyone, and welcome to the community garden workshop. I'm Sarah, the workshop coordinator. Today, we'll discuss planning and problem-solving for our garden. First, let me give you some background. The garden was started three years ago by a group of local residents. We now have 25 members, and we grow vegetables, herbs, and flowers. Our main goal is to provide fresh produce for the community and to create a green space for everyone to enjoy. This shared purpose is what brings us together, and it guides every decision we make about how the garden is used.

Now, let's talk about planning. When planning what to grow, we need to consider the sunlight each area receives. The north side gets less sun, so it's better for leafy greens like lettuce and spinach. The south side is sunnier, perfect for tomatoes and peppers. Also, we should think about crop rotation to avoid pests and diseases. For example, don't plant tomatoes in the same spot year after year. Moving crops between beds helps keep the soil healthy and reduces the risk of problems building up over time.

Next, problem-solving. A common problem is pests. Last year, we had a lot of aphids on the roses. We tried spraying with soapy water, which helped a bit, but the best solution was introducing ladybugs. They eat aphids naturally. Another issue is water. We have a water butt that collects rainwater, but during dry spells, it's not enough. So we're planning to install a drip irrigation system. That should save water and time, and it will make watering much more reliable during the summer months.

Now, I'd like to mention our upcoming events. On the first Saturday of next month, we'll have a planting day. Everyone is welcome to help plant the summer crops. We'll provide tools and seeds. Also, on the last Friday of the month, there's a garden social evening. It's a chance to meet other members and share ideas. Please bring a dish to share if you can.

Finally, a few reminders. Please sign in when you arrive, so we know who's here. And remember to close the gate behind you to keep rabbits out. If you have any questions, feel free to ask me or any of the committee members. Thank you for listening, and enjoy the garden!

Section 3: Week 48 Listening Part 3: Discussing a Group Presentation

TUTOR: Good morning, both. Thanks for coming. So, this is your first tutorial about the group presentation for the environmental science module. How are things going?
STUDENT A (Mia): Well, we've done some research, but we're a bit stuck on how to organise the presentation.
STUDENT B (Leo): Yes, we've got lots of information, but we're not sure what to include.
TUTOR: OK. Let's start with the structure. What's your main argument?
MIA: We want to show that recycling alone isn't enough to solve the plastic problem.
LEO: Actually, I think we should focus more on reducing plastic production. That's the key issue.
MIA: But we agreed to talk about recycling first, didn't we?
LEO: Yes, but I mean the overall message should be about reduction.
TUTOR: That's an important distinction. You can present recycling as one part of the solution, but argue that reduction is more effective. Does that make sense?
MIA: Yes, I think so. So we could compare the two approaches.
TUTOR: Exactly. And you should also consider the limitations of each. For example, recycling rates vary a lot between countries.
LEO: That's true. We found data showing that some countries recycle over 50% of their plastic waste, while others recycle less than 10%.
TUTOR: Good. That's a useful comparison. Now, what about your conclusion?
MIA: We were thinking of recommending a combination of both, but with more emphasis on reduction.
TUTOR: That sounds reasonable. But you need to be careful not to sit on the fence. You should make a clear recommendation.
LEO: So we should say that reduction is the priority, but recycling is still necessary?
TUTOR: Yes, that's a clear position. Now, let's talk about your sources. Have you checked the reliability of your data?
MIA: We used government reports and some academic articles. But we haven't checked the date of all the sources.
TUTOR: You should definitely do that. Older data might not reflect current trends. Also, make sure you cite everything properly.
LEO: OK, we'll do that. What about the presentation itself? How long should it be?
TUTOR: It should be 15 minutes, followed by 5 minutes for questions. And remember, you'll be assessed on your delivery as well as content.
MIA: So we need to practise speaking clearly and making eye contact?
TUTOR: Yes, and also engaging the audience. Don't just read from your slides.
LEO: Got it. One more thing: should we include a handout?
TUTOR: That's optional, but if you do, keep it short—one page maximum. Now, I'd like you to send me your outline by Friday. Can you do that?
MIA: Yes, we can.
LEO: Sure.
TUTOR: Great. And if you have any questions, just email me. Good luck!

Section 4: Independent Listening: Academic Talk on Urban Green Spaces and Well-being

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about urban green spaces and their effects on well-being. This is a topic that has received a lot of attention in recent years, especially as cities grow denser. I'll start with some definitions, then discuss the benefits, and finally consider some of the challenges.

First, what do we mean by 'urban green space'? Generally, it refers to any vegetated area within a city, such as parks, gardens, green roofs, and even street trees. These spaces can be public or private, large or small. For example, a small community garden is just as much a green space as a large city park.

Now, why do green spaces matter for well-being? There is a growing body of evidence suggesting that access to green space is associated with better mental health. For instance, a study in the UK found that people who lived within 300 metres of a park reported lower levels of stress. However, it's important to note that this is a correlation, not necessarily causation. We can't say for sure that the park caused the lower stress; perhaps people who are less stressed choose to live near parks.

Another benefit is physical activity. Green spaces provide opportunities for walking, cycling, and playing. This can help reduce obesity and improve cardiovascular health. But again, the relationship is complex. Some studies show that people who use green spaces regularly are more likely to meet physical activity guidelines. Yet, we must consider that those who are already active might be more inclined to use these spaces.

Social benefits are also significant. Green spaces can serve as meeting places, fostering community cohesion. For example, a community garden can bring neighbours together, creating social ties. This can be particularly important in high-density areas where people might otherwise feel isolated.

However, we should not romanticise green spaces. There are challenges. One issue is maintenance: who pays for the upkeep? Another is safety: some green spaces may be perceived as unsafe, especially at night. Also, green spaces can contribute to gentrification, driving up property prices and displacing lower-income residents. So, while green spaces are generally beneficial, their implementation requires careful planning.

To sum up, urban green spaces offer multiple benefits for well-being, including mental health, physical activity, and social cohesion. But we need to be aware of potential drawbacks and ensure that these spaces are accessible to all. Thank you.

grammar.title: 比较、推测、条件与让步
grammar.explanation: 比较差异时，可以用比较级加 than；修饰可数复数用 fewer，修饰不可数数量用 less。might 加动词原形可以表示不确定的推测。表达将来可能出现的条件，通常在 if 从句用一般现在时，主句用 will 加原形。although 引出让步时，主句不再同时用 but。下面四题使用新的独立句子。
grammar.example: But if it rains, we cancel.
